newsitem.title: FRANCE: GOLF-PARNEVIK AND WOOSNAM SHARE LANCOME TROPHY LEAD.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-PARNEVIK AND WOOSNAM SHARE LANCOME TROPHY LEAD.

text.p: Jesper Parnevik bogeyed the final hole to drop back into a tie with Ian Woosnam for the halfway lead in the Lancome Trophy on Friday.
The U.S.-based Swede carded a one-under-par 69 and Woosnam a 68 on a day of indifferent scoring in swirling winds on the St Nom-la-Breteche course just outside Versailles.
They are both five under for 36 holes.

Colin Montgomerie, battling with Woosnam to head the Order of Merit, chipped in for a birdie at the last with a shot that would have gone 10 feet past the hole if it had not hit the pin and dropped in.

Montgomerie, Europe's leading moneywinner for the past three years and the defending champion here, compiled a 70 that left him just one shot behind on four under, level with Silvio Grappasonni of Italy and fellow Britons Ross Drummond and Peter Baker.
They carded 67, 68 and 69 respectively.

Parnevik, who cannot gain Ryder Cup qualification points here because he is not a full European Tour member, said the private battle between Montgomerie and Woosnam to head the merit list could help him.
"Maybe they'll be battling each other and won't notice me," he said. "But more probably, they'll both try to win and I'll have to play harder."
U.S. Masters champion Nick Faldo improved two shots from his opening 73 to a 71 and safely made the halfway cut which fell at five over.
But he said he was "playing so badly" because of problems with his hip action on his swing.

Italian Costantino Rocca is alone on three under after a 69. Bernhard Langer lost some of the magic he enjoyed with a new broom-handled putter in a 67 on Thursday and slipped to a 71 to stand on two under.
Europe's Ryder Cup captain Seve Ballesteros struggled round in 75, complaining afterwards about poor marshalling of spectators on the course.
"I've been marshalling instead of playing today. It ruined my concentration because it was impossible to play. I complain every year but it does not get better," he said.
Ballesteros, who carded a first round 69, is on four over.
Woosnam was the morning pacesetter, establishing a target which did not appear too daunting on a sunny, mild morning but which proved a challenge later as the wind blew.
He began his round at the 10th and gained a shot at the short 12th with a 12-foot putt.
Like Montgomerie, he also birdied the 18th -- his ninth hole -- and it came with a more orthodox four-iron to the green followed by a 25-foot putt.
He also birdied the second, his 11th, but dropped a shot at the eighth when his drive finished behind a tree.
Afterwards Woosnam suggested Monegomerie had been receiving preferential treatment by being allotted early start times in the opening round, giving him a chance to "get the first punch in".
"He starts first, posts a good score and I feel I have to match it. That puts more pressure on me," Woosnam said.
Tour officials denied it was any more than pure coincidence the draws worked out that way, while Montgomerie quipped: "Good. That means he is worried."
Parnevik, in good form on the U.S. Tour recently, hit his tee shot at the short last hole into a bunker and then missed a six-foot putt at a hole cut on the top of a little ridge.
"A lot of the pin positions were tough today and the swirling wind made it difficult, too," he said.
Montgomerie bogeyed the first two holes and then put together 13 successive pars to the long 16th.
He struck two drivers on to the green there and holed a 20-foot putt for eagle.
"I've never had three better shots than that and to eagle that was super," he said.
But his concentration lapsed at the next and he drove behind a tree to drop a shot, before recovering brilliantly with his chip at the last.
